newsitem.title: FRANCE: French opposition Socialists set economic policy.
newsitem.headline: French opposition Socialists set economic policy.

text.p: France's opposition Socialists adopted policies on Sunday to create jobs, cut working hours and revive the party's fortunes in the run-up to 1998 legislative elections.

"The time for reconquest is starting," party leader Lionel Jospin told about 400 party members at the end of a weekend meeting in a Paris suburb, accusing President Jacques Chirac of sticking to failed austerity policies.

The Socialists endorsed a platform of economic and social policies designed to create 700,000 jobs for young people within two years and a law cutting the working week to 35 hours from 39 with no loss in wages.
The 15-page document also focuses on new housing and renewing decaying cities. In a show of hands, the Socialists voted 304 in favour with 88 abstentions. No one voted against.
Members of the ruling centre-right denounced the plan as a string of empty illusions that would hike taxes and force firms to invest in creating meaningless posts.

"Father Christmas Jospin has nothing in his sack," said Jean-Francois Mancel, secretary-general of the Chirac's Rally for the Rebublic Party. The Socialists say the scheme will not increase the overall tax burden.
"The proposals...are archaic," Defence Minister Charles Millon said, saying they marked a return to an outmoded form of state intervention.

Jospin, a former education minister beaten by Chirac in a run-off for the presidency in May 1995, savaged the centre-right government and employers, saying they failed to apply prescriptions of economic austerity to themselves.
He said the government sought to impose "more constraints for employees and pensioners, fewer obligations and duties for the people who are best off, those with capital."
"Since we're told about the need to make efforts, or agree to sacrifice, how is that the theorists of sacrifice never carry them out?" he asked.
Chirac says austerity is needed partly to help France qualify for a single European currency from 1999. The Socialists also favour the euro.

Seventy-five percent of grassroots party members had already voted for the draft with just 16 percent for a more radical left-wing alternative that would have called for a pause in implementing the single currency and lower retirement ages.

Jospin renewed attacks on Chirac for a television interview last week in which the president pledge to continue with economic austerity and ruled out a government reshuffle despite record unpopularity of Prime Minister Alain Juppe.

Jospin said Chirac failed to concentrate on the key issue of unemployment, and wrongly accused unions and the French people of being too resistant to change "as if it was he, the president, who had elected the people and regretted it".

The Socialists were routed in the last elections in 1993, largely because of rising unemployment and creeping sleaze scandals. With the centre-right now skewered by the same issues, the Socialists reckon they have a chance of a comeback.
